line-of-aisling.description: Aisling and her line, as the copyists kept it.

line-of-the-mason.description: Neachdan the mason and his descendants, from the first fire to the end of the line.

the-division.description: The Roinn: the sharing of the land among the heirs and the shares' long history.

the-ford-gathering.description: The yearly meeting of salt and wool at the ford below the Red Hill, from Raghnall Ceannfhionn's wading to the great gathering of the three thousandth year.

the-keepers-promise.description: The promise of Coimhdeach na Fine, the Keeper of the Kin, and how it was kept or broken.

the-long-years.description: The fading of the long lives of Ailean Mòr's blood, from heirs who counted their years in thousands to rulers who died at the ordinary span of every other household.

the-old-ones.description: The people before the Dia-thìrich, their middens, towers, tally-stones and graves, and how the godkin's households met, traded with and outlasted them.

the-seven-coals.description: The seven coals of the vein: their finding, their lighting, their rule and their failing.

the-stone-kings.description: The Stone Kings of the Age of Ailean and what was remembered of them.

events.title: The vigil and the crowning
events.body: Ailean keeps watch by the seven fires for seven nights, fasting, a night for each coal. On the eighth night the coals are cold, and Caoran comes into the grove with the Tuath Dè about him. He names Ailean Rìgh Chlann nan Dè, king of the godkin, and puts into him the power that was in the coals. Of that power Ailean tells no one while he lives.

events.title: Coinneach follows his brother north
events.body: Coinneach mac Shuibhne, unable to wait out a year of silence, sets off after his brother with a sack of oatcake and a skin of buttermilk, following the roads he judges Ailean must have taken toward the grove of Doire ghlas.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: I. Of the Fires under the Oaks

events.title: The camp beyond the oaks
events.body: Coinneach comes within sight of the seven fires at Doire ghlas and finds he cannot cross into the ring of oaks. Coimhdeach na Fine allows him to camp at the tree-line and no nearer, and he keeps his own vigil there through the seven nights of his brother's watch.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: II. Of the Seven Nights

events.title: Voices heard on the fifth night
events.body: On the fifth night of the vigil Coinneach hears, low under the sound of the fires, what he takes for voices, one of them shaped almost like his brother's speech though fallen into a rhythm Ailean never used. He never swears to more than that he heard something.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: II. Of the Seven Nights

events.title: The grove fills with light
events.body: On the eighth night, when the seven fires go dark together, Coinneach watches the grove of Doire ghlas fill with a light that is not firelight, and sees shapes moving among the oaks. His feet will not carry him past the tree-line to follow them.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: III. Of the Eighth Night

events.title: The six pots left cold
events.body: At dawn the six pots that carried Ailean's fires north are found lying empty on the leaves of Doire ghlas, their turf lids scattered, and the pale stone that held the seventh coal lies among them, giving no light but warm to the touch.

links.label: Same place
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: Coinneach finds his brother warm at dawn
events.body: Ailean walks out of the grove at morning and catches his stumbling brother by the arm. Coinneach feels a warmth in it like a hearthstone long after the fire is swept, and knows before any word is said that the night has changed his brother.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: "They named me king"
events.body: Ailean tells his brother only this much of the night in the grove: that he has been named king. He says nothing of who named him, of what a king might be king of, or of what was put into him, and Coinneach asks no further, having seen enough from outside the trees.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: The brothers turn south
events.body: Ailean gathers the six empty pots onto his shoulder-pole, leaves the pale seventh stone lying uncovered among the leaves of Doire ghlas, and sets out south with his brother, never lighting the six fires again.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: Ailean passes Na Glinn Àrda
events.body: Ailean walks south past the households of Clann na Ceiste in Na Glinn Àrda without turning aside to any hearth, though he has kin enough among them to be fed and questioned there.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: Eleven kin walk south with him
events.body: Households of Clann na Ceiste near Na Glinn Àrda leave byre and field to follow Ailean south, eleven in all, none able afterward to give a better reason than a feeling not to be argued with. The king shares out Coinneach's sack among them on the road.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: IV. Of the Warm Arm and the Road South

events.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings
events.body: Ailean Mòr, crowned in the grove, comes down to the hill where Dùn ìseal now stands and takes it, and brings the households of the valleys about it under his hand: the first kingdom of the godkin. How he won, none who stood against him could say. He throws up the hill's first ring of bank. He is king from that day until his death, and gives the kingship to no one. With him opens the eldest of the spoken king-lists, afterwards called Rìghrean na Cloiche, which names those who held the hill; it gives no lengths of reign, and it is older than the name Dia-thìrich.

events.title: The bare ring in the frost
events.body: Twice on the road south the company sleeps in the open, and both mornings the frost that silvers the field leaves a bare, warm ring the size of a sleeping man where Ailean lay, as it did at his feet in the grove.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: V. Of the Kin Who Followed

events.title: Coinneach keeps the first telling
events.body: Walking south behind his brother, Coinneach turns over what little he saw from outside the ring of oaks and fits it into an account he is careful never to swell beyond what he truly witnessed, the seed of the telling Clann na Ceiste keep of the seven nights.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of the Seven Nights
told_in.section: V. Of the Kin Who Followed

events.title: The lad who brought the water
events.body: The knapper's son of Dùn ìseal is sent to the hill's crown with water for the man who has just taken it unopposed, and is asked his name and whether the spear he carries is his father's best. Told to take it home and to tell his father the king will want a great many more.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: III. Of the Water and the Spear

events.title: The valleys come in to the hill
events.body: Through the first year the households of the valleys about Dùn ìseal come in to the king one after another, unsummoned, bringing hides, pots, and whatever else they judge fitting, and with their gifts their grazing and their old quarrels, for a telling to be held over them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: IV. Of the Households Coming In

events.title: The first judgement on the hill
events.body: Two households of Dùn ìseal bring before the king a strip of pasture each has claimed for a generation. He asks one question, of whose cattle grazed it before the boundary stone was last moved, and gives the strip back in a sentence. Neither household ever brings the matter before him again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: V. Of the First Judgement

events.title: The king's order to the flint-pit
events.body: The flint-pit behind the houses of Dùn ìseal is set, on the king's own word, to cut spearheads by the score rather than as they are needed, the first order of its kind on the hill. The knapper's son is set to the work alongside his father before that year's leaves are down.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: VII. Of the Pit and the Word Kept

events.title: The warmth with no fire
events.body: In the first hard winter on the hill, a girl of Dùn ìseal stands near the king's own untended fire at night and finds herself warmed through though no flame burns close enough to account for it. She keeps the telling to herself for years before it is believed.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: VI. Of the Warmth with No Fire

events.title: The line of the bank pegged in the snow
events.body: In the depth of the same winter the king walks the crown of Dùn ìseal setting ash pegs with his own hand, marking a line that takes in the old byres and ground for houses not yet built. The households break the frozen turf along it through the worst of the frost.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bank of Dùn ìseal

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Ring Pegged in the Snow

events.title: Flint tools finish the bank's ditch
events.body: When the antler mattocks digging the new ditch at Dùn ìseal blunt faster than they can be sharpened in the frost, the flint-pit sends up scrapers of worked stone to finish the work, so that the hill's first bank is cut as much with flint as with iron.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bank of Dùn ìseal

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Ring Pegged in the Snow

events.title: Muireall and Gormshuil brought to the hill
events.body: As the frost breaks a small company comes down from Na Glinn Àrda to Dùn ìseal: Muireall, the king's wife, and Gormshuil, his young daughter, with a few kin and hands beside them. The hill, which had thought the king had no household of his own, falls quiet to let them through the new gate.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: IX. Of Those Who Were Brought Down

events.title: Dòmhnall born within the new bank
events.body: A son is born to Muireall inside the finished bank of Dùn ìseal, the first of the king's children to draw breath on ground he holds, and the hill takes it as a settled thing that the king has come to stay among them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: IX. Of Those Who Were Brought Down

events.title: A spearhead given for nothing
events.body: The knapper cuts a spearhead finer than any he has made that year, for no order and no payment, and sends it up to the king's fire on the birth of the king's son. He will not say why, only that the giving seemed owed.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

told_in.book: Of the Knapper's Son
told_in.section: IX. Of Those Who Were Brought Down

events.title: The bank of Dùn ìseal
events.body: The first earthwork is raised on the hill at Dùn ìseal: a single bank and ditch, enclosing room for some forty houses. It is the oldest defended place of the hill-folk.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The line of the bank pegged in the snow

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Flint tools finish the bank's ditch

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Gormshuil set to keep the gate

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fearchar born on the hill

events.title: Gormshuil set to keep the gate
events.body: A child of eight, Gormshuil is given the gate of the new bank to watch, and takes to naming every face and dog on the hill so her father will have someone to tell him at evening what the day brought. The habit holds her the rest of her life.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The bank of Dùn ìseal

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Autumn

events.title: Fearchar born on the hill
events.body: A second son is born to the king within the new bank of Dùn ìseal and named Fearchar; he is the first of the king's children to open his eyes on the hill itself, and will hold it for his father in his time.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The bank of Dùn ìseal

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: III. Of the Wars of the Valleys

events.title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill
events.body: Beathag Ruadh holds the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands. With her opens a second spoken list, kept in the west. The Red Hill list and the list of the Stone Kings make no mention of each other until late in both.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Word of the red hill's woman

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh

events.title: Word of the red hill's woman
events.body: A salt-fish trader carries word up to Dùn ìseal of a woman holding a red hill on the shore of the great lake in her own right, answering to no king. Gormshuil asks her father whether it means trouble; he tells her trouble comes from nearer at hand.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: I. Of the Watching Child

events.title: Muireall's dying words
events.body: In her last two nights Muireall speaks to her daughter of small things, a comb, a debt owed, and warns that her youngest son Fearchar has a temper that will want watching before it finds him trouble he cannot talk his way out of.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: II. Of Her Mother's Dying

events.title: The king hears three cases the day Muireall is buried
events.body: Two days after Muireall is put in the ground the king comes in from the valleys, stands by the mound, then goes into the hearing-house and gives judgement on three waiting cases before dark. He does not speak her name again where any ear can catch it.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: II. Of Her Mother's Dying

events.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein
events.body: Gormshuil nic Ailein, the king's daughter, holds the hill of Dùn ìseal for her father while he rides beyond it, and the list names her second of the Stone Kings; she is the first woman named in any list on Dia-thìr. She was born before the grove, and has none of the long years. One deed is told of her: in a hard winter she moves the herds of Dùn ìseal down to the warm springs and loses none.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Muireall and Gormshuil brought to the hill

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The drive to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The two fingers that never bent again

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The grandchildren take the king for her son

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil's deathbed question

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Gormshuil dies

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The hill understands na Bliadhnachan Fada

events.title: The drive to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh
events.body: With the hardest winter in living memory emptying the byres and the king three valleys off, Gormshuil drives the standing herds two days through drifted snow to Fuarain Theth Muileann ruadh, walking the whole way herself so no beast's fodder is spent on a rider. She loses none.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Hard Winter and the Warm Ground

events.title: The two fingers that never bent again
events.body: Gormshuil comes off the winter drive with two fingers of her left hand frozen stiff, and wears a glove over them in company from that year to her death without ever speaking of how they were got.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: III. Of the Hard Winter and the Warm Ground

events.title: The king weds Sorcha
events.body: Ailean takes a second wife, Sorcha, a woman of the valleys younger than his own eldest daughter, and the hill notes the matter and does not remark on it aloud, as it has grown used to doing with the king's household.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

events.title: Coinneach's counsel on the bank
events.body: Gormshuil tells Coinneach that her father does not age while she has begun to grey. He tells her what he saw the night the fires went out in the grove, and counsels her to keep from asking her father what it cost him, as he has kept from asking these thirty years.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

events.title: Somhairle born
events.body: Sorcha bears the king a son, Somhairle, in the thirty-eighth year after the grove, the first child of Sorcha's line to be counted among those got after the grove.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

events.title: Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Beathag Ruadh, who held An Cnoc Ruadh by the lake before any of the valleys came in to the king, dies an old woman in her own hall, unsworn and unbeaten; her household keeps the palisade after her and the lake shore does not change its ways for her going.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Beathag Ruadh of the Red Hill

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uisdean born on An Cnoc Ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill by the Lake

events.title: Iain Dubh born
events.body: A second son of Sorcha's, Iain Dubh, is born to the king on the hill, the youngest of Ailean's children to be reckoned among Rìghrean na Cloiche in his turn.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

events.title: Coinneach dies, Sloinneadh a' Chlachair passed whole
events.body: Coinneach mac Shuibhne dies an old man, the first teller of the king's deeds, having taught Gormshuil Sloinneadh a' Chlachair word for word as Coimhdeach na Fine gave it in the grove. She is, after her father, the second on the hill to carry the whole of it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The vigil and the crowning

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: IV. Of the Gate and the Years Between

events.title: The grandchildren take the king for her son
events.body: Gormshuil's own grandchildren, seeing the king young at the gate each autumn beside a bent grey grandmother, take him for her son rather than her father, and she lets the mistake stand rather than make them carry a harder truth too young.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: V. Of the Grandchildren Who Took Him for Her Son

events.title: Gormshuil's deathbed question
events.body: On the second night of her dying Gormshuil asks her father whether it hurts to stay young. He does not answer her in words, and says her name once instead, the way a man says a name he does not expect to say again.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Autumn

events.title: Gormshuil dies
events.body: Gormshuil nic Ailein dies an old woman of eighty-one, the king's eldest daughter and second of Rìghrean na Cloiche. He sits by her a night and a day and helps lift the turf over her with his own hands, as he did for no one since Muireall.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Autumn

events.title: The hill understands na Bliadhnachan Fada
events.body: Watching Gormshuil, who carried her father's stubbornness and stillness but not his years, put into the ground beside a father who looks her grandson's age, the hill understands at last that na Bliadhnachan Fada are the grove's alone, and pass to no child got before it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Gormshuil nic Ailein

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: VI. Of the Last Autumn

events.title: Dòmhnall takes the hill
events.body: Dòmhnall Clachach, seventy-four and looking a young man still, takes up the hearing-house his half-sister held since the grove, and says he supposes he had better learn to count who comes and goes, since no one is left who learned it from the start as she did.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

told_in.book: Of Gormshuil at the Gate
told_in.section: VII. Of Dòmhnall Taking the Hill

events.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones
events.body: Dòmhnall Clachach, a son of the king and third of the Stone Kings, holds the hill after Gormshuil and sets marker stones along the valley below it to part the grazing of Dùn ìseal from its neighbours'. Some stand yet, and are argued over yet.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Dòmhnall born within the new bank

links.label: At the same time
links.title: A spearhead given for nothing

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Dòmhnall takes the hill

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The old men disagree at the setting of the stones

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: A grazing quarrel judged by the stones

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Dòmhnall doubts his own stones

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence

events.title: The old men disagree at the setting of the stones
events.body: As Dòmhnall Clachach walks the eastern boundary with his stone-setters, the old men of neighbouring households cannot agree, standing on the very ground, where a line has always run, for the becks have shifted and their memories have not moved with them.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: I. Of the Setting of the Stones

events.title: A grazing quarrel judged by the stones
events.body: Two households dispute a marker on the eastern slope, each swearing it stands to the wrong side of the old line. Dòmhnall Clachach settles it from his own memory of the setting, and both sides go home certain, for the first time, that a stone remembers better than a grandfather.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: I. Of the Setting of the Stones

events.title: Dòmhnall doubts his own stones
events.body: Walking home from the judgement at the marker, Dòmhnall Clachach understands that he has settled the quarrel only because his own long memory outlasts any old man's, and that the stones, once he is gone from the hill, will have no one left to ask which story is true.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Griogar's household turns back the king's riders

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: II. Of What the Stones Did Not Settle

events.title: Griogar's household turns back the king's riders
events.body: In a valley to the north-west a hard old man called Griogar meets two of the king's riders with spears and no parley, the first household in years to refuse the king's word outright rather than simply keep clear of it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Dòmhnall doubts his own stones

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: III. Of the Wars of the Valleys

events.title: The first named storm
events.body: A tempest comes so great that the eldest spoken king-lists give it a name. The name is lost; only the memory of the naming remains.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Storm damage within the bank of Dùn ìseal

events.title: The shell road broken
events.body: The storm breaks the shell causeway of Seann Warr in three places and floods the marsh behind it with lake water. The Seann-Dhaoine do not mend it, and the broken ends may be seen still.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Word of the broken causeway reaches Dùn ìseal

events.title: Storm damage within the bank of Dùn ìseal
events.body: The first named storm strips the thatch from six houses of Dùn ìseal and levels a seventh to its footings. Dòmhnall Clachach spends the night holding roofs down with rope and his own weight, and the hill loses its summer hay and two sheds of the flint-pit, but no one within the bank.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The first named storm

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: V. Of the Storm

events.title: Word of the broken causeway reaches Dùn ìseal
events.body: Traders driven from their usual road by flooded fords bring Dòmhnall Clachach word that the shell causeway of Seann Warr stands broken in three places, and that the Seann-Dhaoine have watched it stay broken through a winter without coming out to mend it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The shell road broken

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: V. Of the Storm

events.title: Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence
events.body: Labhrainn, elder of an old household on the western slope, refuses the line his own father stood by at its setting, the first quarrel in Dòmhnall Clachach's time that is fought not over ground but over a settling that no longer needs an old man's word to stand.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Dòmhnall Clachach sets the boundary stones

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall sits an evening with Labhrainn

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VI. Of the Household That Stood

events.title: Dòmhnall sits an evening with Labhrainn
events.body: After judging against him, Dòmhnall Clachach rides out to Labhrainn's byre and sits a whole evening over the household's own brewing, asking not about the stone but the ground itself, and gives the old man back in listening something the stones had quietly taken from him.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Labhrainn refuses the boundary of his western fence

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VI. Of the Household That Stood

events.title: Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley
events.body: Riding with a dozen men against the household that turned back his riders, Ailean Mòr's son Fearchar takes a spear through the thigh that will not heal straight, though the wound should by any ordinary reckoning have killed him.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fearchar Bacach

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: IV. Of Fearchar Lamed

events.title: Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste
events.body: Somhairle, a son of Ailean Mòr some hundred and sixty years old and looking fifteen, asks his father for no land and no herds, only leave to live among the households of Na Glinn Àrda and be counted a single mouth at a single hearth.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Somhairle tells Dòmhnall why he wants no share

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VII. Of Somhairle Who Took No Share

events.title: Somhairle tells Dòmhnall why he wants no share
events.body: Visiting his brother in Na Glinn Àrda, Dòmhnall Clachach is told that Somhairle wants to be believed when he names whose son follows whose, once the kin have grown too many for any one hearth to hold the account, and that a man who holds land judges his own kin differently.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Somhairle asks to live among Clann na Ceiste

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VII. Of Somhairle Who Took No Share

events.title: The chair of woven birch is built for Fearchar
events.body: The household carpenters of Dùn ìseal build Fearchar Bacach a chair of woven birch with long carrying-poles, unasked, so that he need no longer hide the leg that never set straight, and he takes to being carried with something like relief.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fearchar Bacach

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Chair of Birch and the Riding North

events.title: Uisdean born on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: A son is born by the lake shore to a household of An Cnoc Ruadh's holding line and named Uisdean; the watch on the palisade marks his birth with a fire on the point, as it marks every birth in that hall.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Beathag Ruadh dies on An Cnoc Ruadh

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill by the Lake

events.title: Fearchar Bacach
events.body: Fearchar Bacach, the lame, a son of the king lamed in his father's wars, holds Dùn ìseal under the king after the storm and after Dòmhnall Clachach, and is carried to the gatherings in a chair of woven birch. He is the first ruler on Dia-thìr remembered for a hurt.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Fearchar Bacach lamed in Griogar's valley

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The chair of woven birch is built for Fearchar

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dòmhnall asks his father for the north

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Fearchar Bacach holds Dùn ìseal as Dòmhnall rides north

events.title: Dòmhnall asks his father for the north
events.body: At a gathering below Dùn ìseal, Dòmhnall Clachach asks Ailean Mòr for ground still unsettled rather than the hill he has held a hundred and fifty years. His father grants him the north and no guidance in how to keep it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fearchar Bacach

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Chair of Birch and the Riding North

events.title: Fearchar Bacach holds Dùn ìseal as Dòmhnall rides north
events.body: Dòmhnall Clachach leaves Dùn ìseal with a company of twelve, and the hill takes his brother Fearchar, already sitting its judgements from the chair of birch, for its holder without a word of dispute.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Fearchar Bacach

told_in.book: Of the Stones in the Valley and the Chair of Birch
told_in.section: VIII. Of the Chair of Birch and the Riding North

events.title: Uisdean Mòr takes An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Uisdean, five-and-twenty, takes up the holding of An Cnoc Ruadh on the western lake shore after those before him, an old line owing nothing to Dùn ìseal or to any king of the hill-folk.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill by the Lake

events.title: Uilleam Faire born on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: A boatwright's son is born on the lake shore in the twelfth year of Uisdean's holding, and grows up believing, as every child of that hill does, that the water below it has always belonged to his own people alone.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill by the Lake

events.title: The households dig the ditch across the neck
events.body: Every household of An Cnoc Ruadh turns out to cut the ditch across the low saddle of ground where the hill's rise meets the land, and to raise the oak palisade on the spoil bank behind it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill by the Lake

events.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill
events.body: Uisdean Mòr, second of the Red Hill list, digs a ditch across the neck of the hill where Cathair dhearg now stands and sets a palisade on it. In his time the palisade burns twice and is twice rebuilt.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Uisdean Mòr takes An Cnoc Ruadh

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Uilleam Faire born on An Cnoc Ruadh

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The households dig the ditch across the neck

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The first burning of the palisade

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Uisdean rebuilds with green oak

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The second burning of the palisade

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Dùghall first walks the whole road to the shore

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Dùghall's father gives up asking

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Uisdean Mòr dies on An Cnoc Ruadh

events.title: Uisdean tells the watch why the wall stands
events.body: Walking the palisade by night with the young Uilleam Faire, Uisdean speaks of na Bliadhnachan Fada of the king and of the valleys brought in to the south and east, and does not say whether An Cnoc Ruadh will swear when its turn comes.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: II. Of Growing to the Watch

events.title: The king's company camps unannounced on the shore
events.body: The king comes west along the lake shore with some two hundred spears at the end of a summer, camps below the hill, and sends up no word of his business to Uisdean or to any of An Cnoc Ruadh's households.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: III. Of the Two Hundred Spears

events.title: The first burning of the palisade
events.body: On the last watch before dawn the new palisade catches along its whole length at once in a low, dark, shining flame that no one on the wall can trace to any torch or spark. The hill beats it out by morning with lake water and green hides.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: III. Of the Two Hundred Spears

events.title: Uisdean rebuilds with green oak
events.body: Rather than wait out a season for seasoned timber, Uisdean sets the households to rebuilding the palisade at once with green oak cut from his own hill, against every carpenter's word of how badly it will burn.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: IV. Of the Long Waiting

events.title: The king's spearmen trade through the winter
events.body: Neither striking camp nor pressing nearer the wall, the king's company fishes the shallows and mends its gear through the winter, and trades salted fish and small goods with households of the hill who find it easier than the long carry round the lake.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: IV. Of the Long Waiting

events.title: Reothadh an Rìgh
events.body: In the early days of an t-Ògmhios, when the year should long since have been past any frost, a single clear night puts a white rime on the whole shore. The hill's old women name it from that morning Reothadh an Rìgh.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: V. Of the King's Frost

events.title: The Red Hill bends the knee
events.body: Ailean Mòr comes west to the Red Hill, where the palisade of Uisdean Mòr has twice burned. Uisdean comes down to the lake shore and kneels to him. The Red Hill keeps its own holders and its own list, and swears to the king and not to Dùn ìseal; so neither list names the other.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Uisdean tells the watch why the wall stands

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The king's company camps unannounced on the shore

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The king's spearmen trade through the winter

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Reothadh an Rìgh

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Uilleam throws the water and never learns whose fire it was

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The king's company departs east

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag born to Dòmhnall Clachach

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The palisade raised a third time in seasoned oak

links.label: Fulfilled by
links.title: Dùn ìseal's reciters tell the swearing fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own list

events.title: The second burning of the palisade
events.body: On the night of Reothadh an Rìgh the green oak takes in the same low, dark flame as before, and burns in less time than seasoned wood had, leaving nothing standing for the households to save.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: V. Of the King's Frost

events.title: Uilleam throws the water and never learns whose fire it was
events.body: Uilleam Faire is first to the second fire with a hide-skin of water, and throws it into the worst of the blaze without saving a hand's-breadth of the wall. He carries the question of whose fire it was the rest of his life.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: V. Of the King's Frost

events.title: The king's company departs east
events.body: Within the month of Uisdean's swearing the king's company strikes its tents and goes back east the way it came, and does not return to the lake shore.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: VII. Of the Two Lists

events.title: Dùghall first walks the whole road to the shore
events.body: Dùghall, nine years old, is let walk the whole three days down to the Seann-Dhaoine's shore with his father for the first time, rather than being turned back with the pack-ponies at the last ridge. He learns the trade is carried by gesture alone, in silence kept on both sides.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: Mòrag born to Dòmhnall Clachach
events.body: A daughter is born to Dòmhnall Clachach in the north country he was given, and is named Mòrag; she is the first of the king's grandchildren to carry na Bliadhnachan Fada, and grows up hard-handed among people who call her father only the stone-cutter's son.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag born on An Cnoc Ruadh

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill Without Salt

events.title: The palisade raised a third time in seasoned oak
events.body: With no company camped below to hurry the choosing of timber, An Cnoc Ruadh rebuilds its wall a third time in properly seasoned oak. It never burns again in Uilleam Faire's lifetime.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: VII. Of the Two Lists

events.title: Dùn ìseal's reciters tell the swearing fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own list
events.body: Word of Uisdean's kneeling reaches Dùn ìseal, whose reciters tell it with the fire, the frost and the shingle scene kept whole, fuller than An Cnoc Ruadh's own spare list ever names it. An Cnoc Ruadh never quarrels with their telling.

links.label: Fulfils
links.title: The Red Hill bends the knee

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: VII. Of the Two Lists

events.title: Dùghall's father gives up asking
events.body: Dùghall's father tells his son that he tried, once, as a young man, to learn a Seann-Dhaoine word for the goods they traded, and was met with a courtesy that would not be moved. He has not asked again in forty years, and tells Dùghall which questions the shore means to answer.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: I. Of the Road by Gesture

events.title: The road passes to Dùghall
events.body: Dùghall's father, too heavy in the knees for the bog-causeway, hands the whole carrying road to his son. Dùghall walks it alone that year with a string of ponies his in all but the naming, three days down to the shore and three days back.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: II. Of the Marks at the Midden's Edge

events.title: Strokes on the midden stones
events.body: The Seann-Dhaoine begin to cut single strokes on flat stones set at the edges of their middens, one stone to a household. The strokes are not the script. They are simpler: a mark, and then another.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The road passes to Dùghall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The strokes on the midden stones are first counted

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Dùghall carries the question home unanswered

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dùghall takes his grandson down for the last time

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dùghall trades for less on his last shore

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Dùghall dies on the hill

events.title: The strokes on the midden stones are first counted
events.body: Dùghall, three-and-twenty, notices that the flat stones set at the edge of one household's midden carry cut strokes, one or two to a stone, and that their number has grown by a few since he first began to notice them. He can get no answer to what they are, by word or by gesture.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: III. Of the Stroke Cut After a Burial

events.title: Dùghall carries the question home unanswered
events.body: Dùghall tells his father what he has seen at the midden's edge. His father says he saw the same stones himself, years before, and had already judged them a question the shore did not mean to answer, and had stopped asking it.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: II. Of the Marks at the Midden's Edge

events.title: Uisdean Mòr dies on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: Uisdean dies in his own bed on the hill in his eighty-seventh year, two-and-twenty years after the swearing, having outlived the fire, the frost and the king's two hundred spears.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Uisdean Mòr of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of the Palisade that Burned Twice
told_in.section: VII. Of the Two Lists

events.title: The counting of the dead begins
events.body: The Seann-Dhaoine, whoever they were, who built Làrach an Dùin-fhaire and Làrach an Dùin, begin to keep count of their dead. They keep it before ever there were Dia-thìrich to take up the custom.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A household mourns behind a wall of turf

links.label: Answered by
links.title: A fresh stroke is cut beneath an old one

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Dùghall counts every ridge on the shore

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Dùghall keeps the counting stones from his sons

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The grandson counts the ridge and loses the count

events.title: A household mourns behind a wall of turf
events.body: Dùghall, come down to the shore in his sixty-seventh year, wakes in the night to low voices shaped like no ordinary talk, and to boats kept ashore past their hour. He does not go out while it lasts, having learned from the hill's own griefs not to.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The counting of the dead begins

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: III. Of the Stroke Cut After a Burial

events.title: A fresh stroke is cut beneath an old one
events.body: The morning after the low voices, Dùghall finds a second stroke cut fresh beneath the single old one on the newest of the midden stones, and understands, all at once, that the Seann-Dhaoine mark the going of their own dead the way a hill household marks a grave.

links.label: Answers
links.title: The counting of the dead begins

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: III. Of the Stroke Cut After a Burial

events.title: Dùghall counts every ridge on the shore
events.body: Dùghall walks the whole shore that morning and finds every household keeps its own ridge of stones the same way, some bearing a single stroke, some bearing more than he can easily count. He carries the understanding home and tells his father, who is glad, at the last, to have the answer he had stopped seeking.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The counting of the dead begins

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: Dùghall keeps the counting stones from his sons
events.body: Dùghall says nothing more of the midden stones to his sons as they take up the road at his shoulder, judging that each will come to the ridge himself in his own year, as he had. He judges rightly.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The counting of the dead begins

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: Dùghall takes his grandson down for the last time
events.body: One-and-seventy, and carrying the road no more himself, Dùghall takes his eldest son's boy down to the shore, both understanding without saying so that it is his last going. He finds two houses fallen roofless and fewer threads of smoke than he has ever counted there before.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: The grandson counts the ridge and loses the count
events.body: Dùghall sets his grandson to count the stones of the oldest ridge, and the boy loses the count twice among stones fallen and half-sunk in the turf. Dùghall tells him it is no bad thing to meet a count a man cannot finish, if the count is an honest one.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The counting of the dead begins

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: Dùghall trades for less on his last shore
events.body: Dùghall trades what hides he carried for less than the same weight once brought, and walks the three days home with his grandson bearing, unknowing, the whole weight of what the old man had carried down that road alone for two-and-sixty years.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: Dùghall dies on the hill
events.body: Dùghall Ceannaiche dies on the hill that winter, an old man by any hill reckoning, and it is his grandson who takes up the packs the next summer and walks south alone, counting the midden stones before he trades a single hide, as the old man had taught him.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Strokes on the midden stones

told_in.book: Of the Strokes on the Midden Stones
told_in.section: IV. Of the Grandson and the Fewer Hearths

events.title: The tally wall of Seann Warr
events.body: At the eastern Seann Warr the counting stones are built into a wall, each cut with its strokes, some three thousand strokes in all. The wall grows for many lifetimes.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The king rides east with Somhairle to Seann Warr

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Somhairle first sees Balla nan Stràc

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The king's stillness at the wall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Somhairle sets Balla nan Stràc in the Line

events.title: The king rides east with Somhairle to Seann Warr
events.body: The king summons his son down from Na Glinn Àrda and rides the coast road east to Seann Warr with a small company. Somhairle, three hundred and fifty-one years old and near two hundred years among Clann na Ceiste, sees the shore he has only ever heard recited.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tally wall of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: I. Of the Road East

events.title: Somhairle first sees Balla nan Stràc
events.body: At the midden's edge of Seann Warr, Somhairle walks the whole length of the counting stones with his father and finds them built into a wall past any easy counting, the oldest courses run together into a single grey weight of strokes.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tally wall of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: I. Of the Road East

events.title: The king's stillness at the wall
events.body: The king stands a long while at the oldest of the tally stones with his hand flat against it, and tells Somhairle only that the wall has stood longer than the bank at Dùn ìseal, and perhaps longer than the grove. He says no more of it that day.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The tally wall of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: I. Of the Road East

events.title: Somhairle sets Balla nan Stràc in the Line
events.body: Somhairle adds his first telling of his own to Sloinneadh a' Chlachair: the wall at Seann Warr, some three thousand strokes, grown over many lifetimes. It is the first fact he ever sets down unaided, and he keeps it carefully all his life.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The tally wall of Seann Warr

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: I. Of the Road East

events.title: The count at Seann Tarr
events.body: The counting comes to Seann Tarr in the north-east. There the stones are cut with strokes in fives and set in the floor of a house, and the house is lived in over its own dead.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Somhairle finds the house over the dead at Seann Tarr

events.title: Somhairle finds the house over the dead at Seann Tarr
events.body: Sent north on a grazing dispute, Somhairle walks down to Seann Tarr and finds a household living in a long low house whose floor is paved with dressed slabs cut with strokes in fives. He does not enter, and sets the custom down without asking after it.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The count at Seann Tarr

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: II. Of Seann Tarr and the House over the Dead

events.title: A carrier brings word the strokes run thick
events.body: A carrier of hides tells Somhairle at a ford, in passing, that the tally stones are cut thicker that year than any season he has known, and thicker at all three shores at once. Somhairle rides to Seann Warr and Seann Tarr within the month and finds it true.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The bad years in the counts

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: III. Of the Thickening

events.title: The bad years in the counts
events.body: The tally stones at Seann Warr, Seann Tarr and Seann Chwen thicken together: more strokes to each stone, more stones to each course. Death comes on three coasts at once. What it was the strokes do not tell.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: A carrier brings word the strokes run thick

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The king's one visit to the wall

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Somhairle sets the thickening in the Line

events.title: The king's one visit to the wall
events.body: The king rides to Seann Warr with a small company and walks Balla nan Stràc alone, his hand against the newest stone for the better part of a morning. Asked by his son what he saw, he answers only, "A people counting," and speaks of it to no one again.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The bad years in the counts

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: III. Of the Thickening

events.title: Somhairle sets the thickening in the Line
events.body: Somhairle records the king's visit to the wall in the fewest words the Line will bear: that the king stood long before it and, asked what he saw, said only that he had seen a people counting. He adds no explanation of his own.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The bad years in the counts

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: III. Of the Thickening

events.title: The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen
events.body: At the Seann Chwen near Cuan dhearg the last tally stone is left half-cut: two strokes finished, a third begun and forsaken. The chisel marks stop in mid-groove.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Somhairle finds Clach nan Dà Stràc at Seann Chwen

events.title: Somhairle finds Clach nan Dà Stràc at Seann Chwen
events.body: Word of an unfinished stone reaches Na Glinn Àrda, and Somhairle rides two days south to Seann Chwen, quieter than either shore he knew. He finds the newest tally stone left with two strokes finished and a third abandoned mid-groove, the chisel marks stopped clean.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The half-cut stone of Seann Chwen

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: IV. Of the Half-Cut Stone

events.title: The last smoke seen at Seann Tarr
events.body: The carrier who first brought word of the thickening finds Seann Tarr's house over the dead standing open and cold, its hearth unlit, the household gone without any sign of where. Somhairle rides down the following spring and finds the whole shore silent.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: V. Of the Silence

events.title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent
events.body: After the half-cut stone no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated. Their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and their script is cut no more. How they ended no telling knows.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The last smoke seen at Seann Tarr

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Somhairle rides the three shores in one circuit

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Somhairle sets down the Silence

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The hill-folk find the coasts wholly empty

events.title: Somhairle rides the three shores in one circuit
events.body: In a single season, the first any reciter has made the round, Somhairle rides from Seann Warr to Seann Tarr and down to Seann Chwen and finds all three the same: middens grown over, boats rotted on their keels, turf houses softening back into the ground.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: V. Of the Silence

events.title: Somhairle sets down the Silence
events.body: Somhairle enters the shortest of his four tellings in the Line: that after Clach nan Dà Stràc no work of the Seann-Dhaoine can be dated, their middens stop growing, their harbours silt, and how they ended, the telling does not know.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: V. Of the Silence

events.title: The hill-folk find the coasts wholly empty
events.body: By this year no hill trader who once walked the three shores still finds a fire lit on any of them. The households who might have answered a knock are themselves gone, and carriers give the roads over to shores that no longer answer.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The Seann-Dhaoine fall silent

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: V. Of the Silence

events.title: Somhairle weds Cairistìona
events.body: Somhairle marries Cairistìona of Na Glinn Àrda, a shepherding household's daughter of no house of Clann na Ceiste, before both their fires at the turn of the year. He sets nothing of the wedding itself in the Line, judging it a thing that belongs to the man and not to the telling.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Ailean Mòr, first of the Stone Kings

told_in.book: Of the Tally Wall and the Half-Cut Stone
told_in.section: VI. Of Cairistìona

events.title: Word of Beathan's birth reaches the river households
events.body: News that Somhairle and Cairistìona have a son, Beathan, and that the boy will be kept among Clann na Ceiste in the high pastures rather than brought to the hill, travels down every settled valley by the ordinary traffic of drovers and salt-carriers. It reaches Iain mac Fhearchair's household on the Abhainn naomh the same week as the shearing.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The old names kept

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: I. Of the Word Seann

events.title: The hill-folk of the upper Abhainn naomh first say Seann Skell
events.body: Iain mac Fhearchair's generation on the river inherits, without ever deciding it as a household, the custom of naming the Seann-Dhaoine's old places with the plain word for old set before them. Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen and Seann Skell pass into ordinary speech as though no other names had ever been possible.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The old names kept

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: I. Of the Word Seann

events.title: The old names kept
events.body: The hill-folk keep the names of the Seann-Dhaoine places and set before them only their own word for 'old': Seann Dunn, Seann Chwen, Seann Skell and the rest. They turn nothing into their own tongue, and the roots of those names are not understood.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Word of Beathan's birth reaches the river households

links.label: Caused by
links.title: The hill-folk of the upper Abhainn naomh first say Seann Skell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain forbids his household the tower before any of them have seen it

events.title: Iain forbids his household the tower before any of them have seen it
events.body: Iain mac Fhearchair, recalling a single visit to the coast as a young man, tells his daughter Marsaili and the rest of his household that no good comes of taking up what the Seann-Dhaoine left lying, and names the tower at the harbour's mouth as a thing never to be entered, years before the household has any plan of settling near it.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old names kept

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: I. Of the Word Seann

events.title: Three river households crowd one bend
events.body: Grazing on the middle Abhainn naomh, held by one household in Iain's father's day, now feeds three grown from it, and the quarrels over the bend grow more frequent than the grass allows for. Iain begins to speak of the empty coast as a way out of them.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

events.title: Iain calls the household to the coast
events.body: On a dark-half evening Iain mac Fhearchair tells his household plainly that he means to move it to the empty harbour at Seann Skell before another winter turns, judging a shore with good landing and no claimant better than another forty years of quarrelling over the river bend.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

events.title: The old landings taken up
events.body: Families of the hill-folk come down the Abhainn naomh and settle in the empty river harbour at Seann Skell, using the old mole and mending none of it. They are not known to have dwelt by the water before.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Three river households crowd one bend

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Iain calls the household to the coast

links.label: Answered by
links.title: Eleven souls come down the Abhainn naomh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain marks the ground and forbids the tower again

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The household mends the mole with stone it did not take

links.label: Leads to
links.title: A winter storm breaks the seaward mole

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain refuses to build with the broken stone

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The mole stands whole again

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The first hill-folk boats put out from Seann Skell

links.label: Answered by
links.title: Marsaili sees the mole's true shape from the water

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Tormod born to Iain Dubh

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Iain mac Fhearchair dies at the harbour

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The sea takes its first life at Seann Skell

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Marsaili chooses the plain burial

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Word of the king's word reaches Marsaili third-hand

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Marsaili nic Iain dies at Seann Skell

events.title: Eleven souls come down the Abhainn naomh
events.body: Iain mac Fhearchair's household, eleven souls with ox-carts and what beasts they can drive, follows the Abhainn naomh two days further than any of them has gone, and comes out above the tide to find the harbour at Seann Skell standing exactly as the traders had always described it: empty, the old mole running into the flood, the tower blind-walled by the water.

links.label: Answers
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

events.title: Iain marks the ground and forbids the tower again
events.body: Before the household sleeps its first night at the harbour, Iain walks the ground himself and sets a line of stones marking where a house may be built and where it must not, keeping every wall a household's length from the nearest standing Seann-Dhaoine wall and the whole camp further still from the tower.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

events.title: The household mends the mole with stone it did not take
events.body: The household repairs the landward stretch of the old mole with stone gathered fresh from the shore, never lifting a stone already laid by the Seann-Dhaoine, a distinction Iain draws carefully and his children keep after him without ever quite putting into words.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: II. Of the Coming to the Harbour

events.title: A winter storm breaks the seaward mole
events.body: In the first days of an Fhaoilleach a storm out of the west drives the tide higher up the shingle than any of the household remembers from their river years, and breaks the oldest, untouched stretch of the mole, scattering its stones along the shore.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: III. Of the Storm and the Cracked Stone

events.title: Iain refuses to build with the broken stone
events.body: Two of Iain's sons-in-law argue that stone the sea itself has thrown down is no longer bound by the household's rule against taking up Seann-Dhaoine work. Iain refuses them, holding that the storm's breaking gives the household no claim the storm did not also give, and the mole is mended instead with new-quarried stone.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: III. Of the Storm and the Cracked Stone

events.title: The mole stands whole again
events.body: After two summers of quarrying and hauling stone down from the higher ground, the mended mole stands sheltered end to end, and no household on that shore again seriously argues for lifting a Seann-Dhaoine stone to lay it elsewhere.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: III. Of the Storm and the Cracked Stone

events.title: The first hill-folk boats put out from Seann Skell
events.body: Tearlach mac Ghilleonain and two of Iain's grandsons build the first boats the harbour has held since it was last worked, small hide craft trusted for the first time to open tide, and Marsaili herself goes out in the first of them on a calm morning her father judges safe.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Marsaili sees the mole's true shape from the water
events.body: Looking back at the harbour from beyond the mole's mended length, Marsaili understands for the first time that the household's hurried repairs had done little more than follow, stone for stone, a plan the Seann-Dhaoine had already laid according to the set of the tide, and tells her father so that evening.

links.label: Answers
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Tormod born to Iain Dubh
events.body: A son is born to Iain Dubh at Dùn ìseal and named Tormod; he grows slowly, as the grove's grandchildren grow, and will stand at his father's cairn a young man of eighty-seven still holding nothing of his own.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Shingle at Baile ghorm
told_in.section: III. Of the Cairn on the Hill

events.title: Iain mac Fhearchair dies at the harbour
events.body: Iain mac Fhearchair, who led his household down from the river and set the rule against touching what the Seann-Dhaoine left standing, dies at Seann Skell eleven years before the sea takes its first life among his people, and his daughter Marsaili holds the household in his place.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: The sea takes its first life at Seann Skell
events.body: A young man of Tearlach mac Ghilleonain's house drowns in a squall too sudden for any boat then on the shore to outrun. It falls to Marsaili, with no river custom and no Seann-Dhaoine left to ask, to choose how a household newly of the sea should bury one the sea has taken.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Marsaili chooses the plain burial
events.body: Marsaili buries the drowned man on the rise above the shingle in the plain hill fashion of her mother's grave on the river, judging that a household too new to the shore has no business inventing rites for it, and wronging no one, living or dead, by the choice.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Word of the king's word reaches Marsaili third-hand
events.body: A household two harbours south tells and retells what little the king said of Seann Skell in passing, riding the coast road with three men: that he had heard the hill was settling an empty shore and thought it well, and would send no one to tell them how to hold it. Marsaili hears it thinned by retelling and asks for no more of it.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Seonag born on An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: A daughter is born to the holder of An Cnoc Ruadh and named Seonag; she learns the tallies of the salt before she can reach the drying-platform, and will carry a pebble bag for them all her life.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Mòrag born to Dòmhnall Clachach

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

events.title: Marsaili nic Iain dies at Seann Skell
events.body: Marsaili, who led the household's boats before any other hand had proved the harbour safe and buried its first drowned man in the plain hill way, dies the first of her father's line to be laid within sight of the sea, on the same rise above the shingle as the young man who went before her.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The old landings taken up

told_in.book: Of the Old Names
told_in.section: IV. Of the Boats and the Burial

events.title: Mòrag judges the empty salt trade a war in waiting
events.body: Mòrag Chruaidh hears the third salt-trader in a summer return empty-handed from the southern shore and judges aloud, in her father's hall, that a household with salt and no king and a household with a king and no salt cannot go on as they are, and resolves to go south herself rather than wait a season for word to reach Dòmhnall in the north.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: I. Of the Hill Without Salt

events.title: Eleven spears go south by the drovers' track
events.body: Mòrag takes eleven men south along the coast track the hill's own herders use to drive beasts to winter grazing, telling them on the road that the raid is to take salt and nothing more: no house burned, no beast lifted beyond a needed ox, no blood shed that the salt-folk do not themselves choose to shed defending it.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: II. Of the Shingle at Baile ghorm

events.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid
events.body: Mòrag Chruaidh, the king's granddaughter and fifth of the Stone Kings, raids the salt-pans on the southern shore at Baile ghorm, which do not yet own the king, and carries off the salt. It is the first war in either list. Seven fall on the hill side, and the number is kept.

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Mòrag judges the empty salt trade a war in waiting

links.label: Caused by
links.title: Eleven spears go south by the drovers' track

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Donnchadh Bàn falls at the shelters

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag turns back once on the strand

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: The seven of the raid named at the hill

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Màiri hears the seven names of Mòrag's raid

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh dies

events.title: Donnchadh Bàn falls at the shelters
events.body: Donnchadh Bàn, Mòrag's father's oldest belted man, is the first of the seven to fall in the raid on the salt-scrapes at Baile ghorm, cut down at the mouth of the turf shelters as the salt-folk come down onto the shingle.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: III. Of the Bank Behind the Shingle

events.title: Mòrag turns back once on the strand
events.body: With the salt loaded and her people falling back up the strand, Mòrag turns once before full light to look at her seven dead among the stones, and resolves that their names will not be let go the way a lost beast or a broken tool is let go.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: II. Of the Shingle at Baile ghorm

events.title: The seven of the raid named at the hill
events.body: At the turn of the winter after the raid, on the night the hill keeps for its dead, Mòrag stands at her father's hearth and names all seven who fell at Baile ghorm aloud, in the order they fell, beginning the naming that the hill goes on keeping at the same fire every year after.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Mòrag Chruaidh and the salt-flats raid

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: III. Of the Bank Behind the Shingle

events.title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm
events.body: Shallow clay basins are made behind a shingle bar at Baile ghorm, the first salt-works of the island. From this time their salt is found in the hill settlements.

links.label: Leads to
links.title: The salt-folk raise a bank behind the pans

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Word of the bank reaches the reciters as an answer

events.title: The salt-folk raise a bank behind the pans
events.body: Within two summers of Mòrag's raid the folk of Baile ghorm raise a bank of shingle and turf behind the tide line and dig shallow clay-lined basins inside it, a means of making salt by sun and wind alone that needs no fire a raider can find burning in the dark.

links.label: Follows from
links.title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: III. Of the Bank Behind the Shingle

events.title: Word of the bank reaches the reciters as an answer
events.body: Traders who carry the first news of the clay basins up the valley road to Dùn ìseal understand, and say to each other more freely than they say to Mòrag herself, that the bank behind the shingle was raised as much against the hill's spears as against the sea.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The salt-pans of Baile ghorm

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: V. Of the Years That Followed

events.title: Seonag of the Red Hill
events.body: Seonag nic Uisdein holds the Red Hill. The list sets her 'after her father', as it sets every holder of Uisdean Mòr's line, though she was born more than three hundred years after he died. It is told that she counted her people by pebbles in a bag, one to a household, and knew by the weight when a household was gone.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: The king hears the raid from Mòrag's own mouth

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Mòrag rides west to An Cnoc Ruadh

links.label: Same place
links.title: Seonag weighs the pebble bag before the king

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Mòrag rides home weighing a different holding

links.label: Leads to
links.title: Seonag of An Cnoc Ruadh dies

events.title: The king hears the raid from Mòrag's own mouth
events.body: Riding down to Dùn ìseal with a small company, the king hears the whole of the salt raid from Mòrag herself and tells her plainly that the south is not yet his to forbid or to avenge, neither blaming nor praising what she has done.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Seonag of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

events.title: Mòrag rides west to An Cnoc Ruadh
events.body: The king takes Mòrag with him on the long ride west to An Cnoc Ruadh, saying little of his purpose, so that she comes to the lake shore not knowing why she has been brought, only that she has been brought to see something.

links.label: At the same time
links.title: Seonag of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

events.title: Seonag weighs the pebble bag before the king
events.body: Seonag nic Uisdein meets the king at her own gate and weighs the worn bag that holds one pebble for every household of An Cnoc Ruadh's shore, and the king weighs it after her and says he is content, the whole business settled without a word of tribute asked or given.

links.label: Same place
links.title: Seonag of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

events.title: Mòrag rides home weighing a different holding
events.body: On the road back east Mòrag turns Seonag's pebble bag over in her mind against her own eleven spears and seven dead, and never again raises a raid, though she never tells anyone plainly that the pebble bag is the reason.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: Seonag of the Red Hill

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: IV. Of the Red Hill and the Pebble Bag

events.title: The first pots at Doire shean
events.body: Pots of coiled clay, fired in open bonfires, are first made at Doire shean on the south-west coast. Within a few lifetimes the whole southern shore uses them.

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Two of the first pots reach Dùn ìseal

events.title: Two of the first pots reach Dùn ìseal
events.body: A trader carries word of the new coiled clay pots fired at Doire shean up to Dùn ìseal, glad for once to be carrying news rather than salt, and Mòrag has two of the first pots set on her own hearth, where they outlast her holding of the hill.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The first pots at Doire shean

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: V. Of the Years That Followed

events.title: The dug-out at Cidhe Beag
events.body: A boat hollowed from a single oak trunk, long enough for six, is sunk and left at the landing on Abhainn uaine now called Cidhe Beag. No older boat on Dia-thìr is known in its whole shape.

links.label: Legacy of
links.title: Word of the dug-out at Cidhe Beag reaches the hill

events.title: Word of the dug-out at Cidhe Beag reaches the hill
events.body: Word of the oak dug-out sunk and left at the landing at Cidhe Beag, the first boat of its kind hollowed whole rather than built plank by plank, reaches Mòrag by the same slow road that carries most new things to whoever holds Dùn ìseal, though she never sees the boat itself.

links.label: Legacy
links.title: The dug-out at Cidhe Beag

told_in.book: Of Mòrag the Hard
told_in.section: V. Of the Years That Followed

events.title: Iain Dubh takes the hill from Mòrag's hand
events.body: Mòrag gives up Dùn ìseal to Iain Dubh, a son of the king older than she is by every reckoning but younger to look at, judging that a holder is ill served by staying past the age when she still has something to learn from the holding.
